records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox page for Buxus microphylla. The page's "Poisonous to Humans" block reads: Poison Severity: Low (this severity is human-scoped, from that heading; the page banner says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."). Poison Symptoms: "Skin irritation minor or lasting only for a few minutes. If ingested, can cause nausea, diarrhea, dizziness and vomiting. Dogs and cats: vomiting, diarrhea; Horses: colic, diarrhea, respiratory failure, seizures". Poison Toxic Principle: Steroidal alkaloids. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Bark, Leaves. The page's Problems list is: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses (tags #problem for cats #problem for dogs #problem for horses). Plant Type: Perennial, Shrub. The pet scoping comes from the Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs entries and the dogs-and-cats symptom clause; horses are listed separately with a different symptom set. RHS's dedicated Buxus microphylla profile has a Potentially harmful row reading "Pets (dogs): Harmful if eaten", followed by a referral to the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and contact numbers regarding pets; RHS names dogs only and gives no line for people or cats, so its scope is narrower than NC State's (people at Low severity, plus cats, dogs and horses). Neither source states a handling warning beyond NC State's contact-dermatitis line. ASPCA's boxwood record is genus-level Buxus spp. and is not an admissible source here.
unknowns: Sources checked: NC State's dedicated page is the anchor for every value. RHS's dedicated profile (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/2571/buxus-microphylla/details) loads and supplies no value for a null field: its hardiness rating 'H6' is a survival rating, not a damage onset; its pH row 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' accepts alkaline soils, so no bound can be set; its Moisture row is the bare 'Well–drained'; its Position row reads 'Full sun, Partial shade'; its Max Height and Max Spread are both '1-1.5 metres' (39-59 in) while its description says 'shrub to 75cm high', so NC State's Dimensions block stays the size anchor; and its Cultivation line warns 'preferably in light shade though will tolerate full sun; in dry soils this can lead to dull foliage and scorching.' MoBot's dedicated Plant Finder page (taxonid=278322) renders in a browser but fails the sandboxed fetcher on its TLS certificate chain, so none of its text is cited; the auditor read it in a browser and reports 'Common Name: boxwood' (the name this catalog holds for Buxus sempervirens), 'Height: 3.00 to 4.00 feet' and 'Spread: 2.00 to 4.00 feet' (matching NC State), 'Sun: Full sun to part shade', 'Water: Medium' (mid-scale, no cadence), and 'Plants prefer soils with a pH of slightly acidic to slightly alkaline.' (no figures), and the warning 'When grown in full sun, plant foliage is more likely to scorch, bronze in winter or suffer from mite attacks.' Full sun stays in outdoor_sun_exposure because NC State's Light field, RHS's Position field and MoBot's Sun field all list it; the scorch cautions are recorded here, not encoded. Clemson's genus-level boxwood factsheet returned 403, and UF/IFAS's Buxaceae topic lists only the Buxus sempervirens sheet (FP080). The temperature, humidity, light-intensity, pH, watering, fertilizing and chill-damage fields therefore stay null.

is_houseplant is false: NC State gives Plant Type Perennial and Shrub and USDA zones 6a-9b, and RHS rates it H6. The container use NC State mentions ('Grow it in a container, along a border, or as an edging or hedge.'; its Landscape Location field includes Patio) and RHS lists ('Patio and container plants') is outdoor container growing. No admissible page describes indoor or houseplant culture.

water_regime is null: NC State's only moisture statements are the Soil Drainage tags (Good Drainage, Moist), the prose 'prefers moist, cool, well-drained soil' with a mulch-to-retain-moisture tip (soil adjective, not a watering instruction), and 'quite drought tolerant' once established (a tolerance trait). No explicit watering statement.
soil_drainage is moderate: NC State's Good Drainage + Moist pair, with the same page warning that poorly drained soils may cause root rot; the mulch tip does not make it moisture_retentive.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State's Soil pH field lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), whose outer bands are open-ended; RHS's dedicated profile gives pH 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', accepting alkaline soils; and MoBot's 'Plants prefer soils with a pH of slightly acidic to slightly alkaline.' (reported by the auditor from a browser read; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited) gives no figures. No floor or ceiling can be set.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light tags are Full sun (6 or more hours) and Partial Shade (2-6 hours), mapped to full_sun and part_shade; prose says full sun to light shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the hour figures in the tag labels are the site-wide legend, not species prose.

NC State files the cultivars 'Wintergreen' and 'Winter Gem' (winter hardy) under this page; Korean boxwood (Buxus sinica var. insularis) is a separate taxon and no hardiness claim from those cultivars was used. No hardiness or chill-damage onset temperature is stated, so chill_damage_f is null. The page lists USDA zones 6a-9b, a range rather than an onset figure.
is_edible is false based on the page's 'Poisonous to Humans' block (ingestion can cause nausea, diarrhea, dizziness and vomiting); no source states any food use.

toxic_to_pets is true on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs entries and its dogs-and-cats symptom clause; the Poison Severity of Low is stated under the human-scoped heading, not for pets.

Mature size is NC State's Dimensions block (Height 3-4 ft = 36-48 in; Width 2-4 ft = 24-48 in). The page's 'Available Space To Plant' of 3 feet-6 feet is a separate planting-space field and was not used.
NC State's page lists Buxus microphylla 'often confused with' Ilex crenata, which was not used as evidence for anything.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Juniperus chinensis has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags. Its tags include "contact dermatitis". Its Edibility field reads: immature cone "berry" used as seasoning. Its Fruit Value To Gardener field reads "Edible", and its Fruit Description says the female cones are blue, fleshy "berry" looking and edible, often used as a seasoning. Its Description adds "The immature berries are often used in cooking for seasoning." The edibility is therefore scoped to the immature female cones used as seasoning; nothing is stated about other parts. RHS's "Potentially harmful" field says: Harmful if eaten/skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. That RHS wording names no animal. The two admissible sources disagree on eating: NC State presents the immature cones as a seasoning, while RHS says the plant is harmful if eaten. No admissible page names cats or dogs, so toxic_to_pets is null.
unknowns: is_edible is null, not true (landing decision under the catalog's edibility rule). NC State's page says "The immature berries are often used in cooking for seasoning.", its Edibility field reads 'immature cone "berry" used as seasoning', its Fruit Value To Gardener field reads Edible, and its Fruit Description calls the female cones "berry" looking and edible, often used as a seasoning. RHS's page for the same species says "Harmful if eaten/skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling", and NC State's tags carry #contact dermatitis. A seasoning use of the immature cones of an ornamental conifer that an admissible source calls harmful if eaten is a marginal food use, and the app shows is_edible true as 'grown to eat' with no condition, so the field is left null and both statements are carried in toxicity_detail. Nothing about culinary juniper (Juniperus communis) is imported.
toxic_to_pets is null: NC State has no Poison block and no cat/dog tags, and RHS's harmful-if-eaten wording names no animal. No ASPCA entry was found, and ASPCA is not an admissible domain.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead name. RHS's dedicated Taxus × media page leads with Anglo-Japanese yew and lists hybrid yew under Other common names. NC State's dedicated page title parenthetical offers only Foundation Yew and Yew, so plain Yew is not used. NC State's 'Previously known as' field prints Taxus media, but the hybrid sign is kept because the same page describes the plant as an artificial hybrid of English yew and Japanese yew. The requested name Anglojap Yew was not found on any admissible page.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's dedicated Taxus x media page carries a warning banner near the top, "This plant has high severity poison characteristics.", with a See below link to its Poisonous to Humans block; the banner itself states no scope. That block is human-scoped and reads: Poison Severity: High. Poison Symptoms: Nervousness, trembling, slow pulse, pupil dilation, difficult breathing, seizures (dogs), abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, convulsions; may be fatal. Early signs: muscular tremors, dyspnea, seizures in dogs. Poison Toxic Principle: Alkaloid taxine. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Bark, Leaves, Seeds. Separately, NC State's Problems field lists Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses; the cat, dog and horse values are separate from the human-scoped Poison block. Its Plant Type field lists two traits, Poisonous and Shrub. Its Tags row carries 22 tags, among them #poisonous, #problem for dogs, #problem for horses, #problem for cats, #poisonous to livestock, #poisonous if ingested and #poisonous fruits. The #poisonous fruits tag is not matched by the Poison Part field, which lists Bark, Leaves and Seeds and does not list fruit or aril; the page says "Birds eat the aril and disperse the seed.", which is not a statement about human edibility. NC State's page is for the hybrid itself; RHS's page for Taxus × media carries no toxicity information.
unknowns: The name Anglojap Yew was not found on any admissible page: NC State's title parenthetical is (Foundation Yew, Yew), RHS leads with Anglo-Japanese yew, and MoBot's page uses yew as its Common Name. Anglo-Japanese yew was landed as the lead name of the dedicated RHS page.
toxic_to_pets rests on NC State's Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs tags and the dog seizure wording on the hybrid's own page; ASPCA's record is genus-level and not admissible, so it was not used.

is_edible is false and rests on the Poison block of NC State's own page for this hybrid: "Poisonous to Humans: Poison Severity: High. Poison Symptoms: Nervousness, trembling, slow pulse, pupil dilation, difficult breathing, seizures (dogs), abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, convulsions; may be fatal. Early signs: muscular tremors, dyspnea, seizures in dogs. Poison Toxic Principle: Alkaloid taxine. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Bark, Leaves, Seeds." The same page's Tags row carries #poisonous if ingested and #poisonous fruits. No admissible page for this hybrid mentions any food use: NC State says only "Birds eat the aril and disperse the seed.", and RHS's page carries no edibility or toxicity statement, so the edibility rule's null (for a poisonous plant whose pages mention a marginal food use) does not apply. The Poison Part list does not name the fruit or aril; the #poisonous fruits tag does.

water_regime left null: MoBot's structured Water: Medium is mid-scale and its Culture sentence is a soil description, not a watering instruction; NC State gives no watering statement. water_dry_down_target and day-interval fields null for an in-ground shrub.

soil_drainage is null at landing. The researched value, moderate, rested on Missouri Botanical Garden's Culture sentence ('Easily grown in average, medium moisture, well-drained soils in full sun to part shade.'), and MoBot refuses this machine, so the quote checker cannot confirm it and a value may not rest on it alone. NC State's page for the hybrid supports no token by itself: its Soil Drainage field carries the single value Good Drainage, and its Description says "These yews prefer sandy or loamy soils and do not tolerate wet conditions." and "They are drought tolerant.", with "Failure to provide proper drainage can lead to root rot." under its plant problems. That is wet intolerance and drought tolerance, not the moist-but-well-drained reading moderate needs, and 'prefer sandy or loamy soils' is wet intolerance rather than the sharp, sandy requirement fast needs.

outdoor_sun_exposure keeps full_sun and part_shade and leaves out full_shade. NC State's Light field lists only Full sun and Partial Shade. Deeper shade is disclosed, not encoded: NC State lists Heavy Shade under Resistance To Challenges, and MoBot's page (reported by the auditor from a browser read; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited) reads Sun: Full sun to part shade, lists Heavy Shade under Tolerate and says "Tolerates shade and is considered to be an excellent evergreen for shady conditions." Neither structured sun field reaches full shade. MoBot warns "Susceptible to winter burn, particularly in exposed sites." and NC State says "Plant these shrubs in areas that provide protection from winter exposure."; both are winter-siting cautions, not a limit on full sun, which both structured sun fields list. direct_sun_hours_max is null because NC State's hour ranges are the site-wide light legend.

Soil pH, temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizing and chill damage are not stated on any admissible page for this hybrid. RHS's Taxus × media page has no cultivation, sun or soil fields, and its Size section holds only a Time to Maturity row reading No preference, with no height or spread.

Mature size 24-240 inches tall and 24-144 inches wide is the page's range across all cultivars (NC State: height varies by cultivar; Dimensions block gives the same 2 to 20 ft and 2 to 12 ft); individual cultivars are much smaller.

attracts_pollinators null: NC State's Attracts field lists only Songbirds, and MoBot's Attracts field (read in a browser) lists Birds: bird food, not pollination. MoBot's page cannot be fetched from this machine, so its three research citations were dropped at landing, and the audit reported that it, like RHS's page, carries no toxicity text.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and begins Cherry Plum, Mirabelle, Myrobalan Plum, in the same order as the page-title parenthetical; the description prose opens on 'purple leaf plum or cherry plum'. The page attributes the purple foliage to varieties or cultivars of the species, and its 'is often confused with' module includes Prunus domestica. RHS's Prunus cerasifera (F) profile renders cherry plum beneath its H1 and lists mirabelle, myrobalan, myrobalan plum and weeping plum as other common names. Cherry Plum is used because it is the first item of NC State's page-title parenthetical and alphabetized list, and the name RHS's profile leads with.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' block (human-scoped heading): Poison Severity: Medium. Poison Symptoms: 'The pits contain cyanide compounds, which are poisonous. If a couple of pits are accidentally swallowed, it will not cause poisoning. The pits are more poisonous if they are ground up/crushed or the seeds are chewed. Fruit that has not been pitted should not be blended into a smoothie. Symptoms include Gasping, weakness, excitement, pupil dilation, spasms, convulsions, coma, respiratory failure.' Poison Toxic Principle: Cyanogenic glycosides. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Leaves, Seeds, Stems. Separately, NC State's Problems field renders six values (Frequent Disease Problems, Frequent Insect Problems, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Short-lived); the three Problem-for values are tags only, with no symptoms, severity or plant part stated for the animals. Separate Edibility line: 'The fruits are edible and are used in tarts or jellies.' The Poison Part list names Leaves, Seeds and Stems and does not list the fruit. RHS's dedicated Prunus cerasifera page carries no toxicity statement and calls the fruit edible ('An upright, rounded, twiggy, deciduous tree producing small, white flowers in early spring as the leaves open, sometimes followed by edible, red, orange or yellow, plum-like fruit about 2.5cm long'), so no admissible source read here disagrees on scope or edibility.
unknowns: NC State's dedicated Prunus cerasifera page is the anchor for every value. RHS's 'Prunus cerasifera (F)' profile (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/94416/prunus-cerasifera-(f)/details) and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286444, which refuses non-browser clients, so it is not cited) were read by the auditor. Both lead with cherry plum (RHS lists mirabelle, myrobalan, myrobalan plum and weeping plum only as other common names), both call the fruit edible (MoBot: 'Flowers are followed by small edible fruits (to 1” diameter) that are sweet but somewhat tasteless.'), and neither carries any toxicity statement. MoBot's 'Height: 15.00 to 30.00 feet' and 'Spread: 15.00 to 25.00 feet' match NC State's Dimensions; RHS's UK sizes are larger (Max Height '8-12 metres', Max Spread 'wider than 8 metres') and were not used, NC State's Dimensions block being the anchor. No dedicated Clemson page for this species was confirmed.

is_edible is true for the fruit, with NC State's whole condition: its Edibility field reads "The fruits are edible and are used in tarts or jellies.", while its Poisonous to Humans block (Poison Severity Medium; Poison Toxic Principle Cyanogenic glycosides; Poison Part Leaves, Seeds, Stems) says "The pits contain cyanide compounds, which are poisonous. If a couple of pits are accidentally swallowed, it will not cause poisoning. The pits are more poisonous if they are ground up/crushed or the seeds are chewed. Fruit that has not been pitted should not be blended into a smoothie." The leaves, seeds and stems are the listed poisonous parts; the fruit is not listed.
toxic_to_pets rests on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags only. No pet symptom list or severity is given; the Medium severity is human-scoped.

records.name_note: NC State and RHS both have a dedicated page for this exact hybrid. NC State's prose opener calls the plant Yoshino Cherry and RHS's profile gives the common name Yoshino cherry, so that name is used. NC State's page title carries the parenthetical (Japanese Flowering Cherry, Potomac Cherry, Tokyo Cherry, Yoshino Cherry), and the separate Common Name(s) list holds the same four names; both are alphabetized, so Japanese Flowering Cherry comes first in each. Japanese Flowering Cherry is also listed on NC State's Prunus serrulata page, so it is a name shared across two taxa and is not used here; it is the name this catalog already gives Prunus serrulata. NC State says the plant is sometimes cited as Prunus serrulata 'Yedoensis', but parentage and origin are unknown, so no parent species is named. It also says the plant is confused vegetatively with the Kwanzan Cherry, and its structured 'is often confused with' module lists Prunus 'Kanzan' among five entries. NC State writes the hybrid sign as an ASCII x, which is normalised to the multiplication sign.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page has no Poison block, so there is no severity rating, poison-part list, symptom list or handling warning. Its structured Problems field lists Messy, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, and its tag line carries #problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats. Plant Type is Perennial and Tree. These are separate flags only; the page gives no toxic compound or symptoms, and none are imported from any other Prunus record. RHS's dedicated Prunus × yedoensis profile carries no toxicity statement.
unknowns: NC State and RHS both have dedicated pages for this exact hybrid. MoBot's dedicated page (taxonid=286608) exists but fails TLS certificate verification for non-browser clients from this machine, so it is not cited. UF/IFAS's ST523 fact sheet now returns HTTP 410, Clemson returned HTTP 403, and cultivar pages are inadmissible. RHS's Position field lists Full sun only, while NC State's Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade, so part_shade is kept on NC State's structured field (the auditor reports that MoBot's 'Sun: Full sun to part shade' agrees; MoBot is not cited). RHS's Max Height (Higher than 12 metres) and Max Spread (wider than 8 metres) are open-ended and set no size bound.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Perennial and Tree with USDA zones 5a-8b, and RHS rates the hybrid H6. No admissible page describes indoor culture. The research record had left the field null; the landing gate needs a cited true or false.

No admissible source gives a watering cadence. NC State's Moist soil-drainage value is a soil adjective, and MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium' (reported by the auditor from a browser read; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited) is mid-scale and supports no water_regime token, so water_regime and the watering fields are null.
is_edible is null. NC State describes the fruit only as showy black drupes that attract birds, and the tag '#food source summer' is wildlife-oriented. It makes no human-food statement.
humidity_need is null. NC State gives only 'humidity tolerant' and Humidity under Resistance To Challenges, which are tolerance traits and not a need.
The sun field and prose give only 'Full sun (6 or more hours...)' and 'Partial Shade (...2-6 hours)', so direct_sun_hours_max is null because there is no species-specific maximum.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State gives no pH field, and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', which sets no numeric floor or ceiling. No admissible source gives a chill-damage onset, temperature, foot-candle or fertilizer figure; NC State's USDA zones 5a-8b and RHS's H6 are hardiness ratings, not damage onsets.
The toxicity evidence is limited to NC State's Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses tags, with no Poison block, no symptoms and no poison parts. toxic_to_pets=true rests on those tags alone.
NC State's Width range (20-50 ft) is very wide and sits next to an 'Available Space To Plant: 24-60 feet' field; only the Dimensions block is used for size.
NC State states parentage as unknown, so parent species are deliberately not named.

attracts_pollinators true rests on NC State's Attracts field (Butterflies, Songbirds) and RHS's 'Plants for pollinators' tag. NC State's Wildlife Value adds 'Fruits attract birds and tree is larval host to butterflies.', so its butterfly entry is partly a larval-host note; RHS's pollinator tag carries the value independently.

records.name_note: NC State's page for Ilex cornuta lists the synonyms Ilex cornuta var. fortunei and Ilex fortunei under "Previously known as". NC State's page title parenthetical is "(Chinese Holly, Horned Holly)", and RHS titles its page "Ilex cornuta | Chinese holly" with "horned holly" as its other common name, so the two pages agree on Chinese holly as the lead name.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Ilex cornuta rates Poison Severity as Low in its Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped), and the summary box near the top of the page reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Its Poison Symptoms field reads "Minor toxicity. Ingestion may cause vomiting, diarrhea, or other illness in humans." The Poison Toxic Principle is Saponins, the Poison Part is Fruits (the only part listed), and Causes Contact Dermatitis is No. NC State's separate Edibility field says "Use caution. Berries are slightly toxic to humans if eaten in quantity." The same page lists "Spines/Thorns" and "Weedy" under Problems; neither is a toxicity tag. The page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag. RHS's page for Ilex cornuta has a Potentially harmful block that reads "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." Its Pets line repeats the fruit warning and names no cat or dog. Both sources name only the fruit as the part not to be eaten; RHS's glove warning names no plant part, and NC State lists Causes Contact Dermatitis as No. No admissible page names cats or dogs for this species, so toxic_to_pets is null.
unknowns: The Missouri Botanical Garden page for Ilex cornuta (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid 276168) could not be loaded. The server's TLS certificate chain would not verify and I did not bypass verification. It contributes no citation. A search snippet said it calls the plant Chinese holly and gives 8-15 ft, but that is unverified here.
Clemson HGIC returned HTTP 403 for a Chinese holly factsheet URL I guessed. Its holly factsheet is genus-level and was not used.
No dedicated UF/IFAS EDIS or other admissible page for this exact species turned up. The Nellie R. Stevens page is a hybrid and the UGA hollies article is multi-species, so neither was used.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page is headed Dasiphora fruticosa, and its 'Previously known as' field lists Pentaphylloides fruticosa and Potentilla fruticosa. The admissible sources split on the genus: RHS's dedicated page for this shrub has the H1 Potentilla fruticosa with Name Status 'Correct'; this record follows NC State's current name. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Bush Cinquefoil, Golden Hardhack, Prairie Weed, Shrubby Cinquefoil, Shrubby Potentilla), and the page-title parenthetical shows the same order. NC State's Description opens with 'Shrubby cinquefoil' and RHS's subtitle beneath its H1 reads 'shrubby cinquefoil', so that is the landed name. Golden Hardhack is not used: RHS lists 'golden hardhack, hardhack, prairie weed, widdy' as other common names, and Hardhack is also an entry in NC State's Common Name(s) list for Spiraea tomentosa, which this catalog lands as Steeplebush. NC State's 'often confused with' module for this species names Potentilla indica. No data was taken from herbaceous Potentilla pages or from Potentilla indica.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's dedicated Dasiphora fruticosa page has no Poison block, so it names no poison part, symptom, toxic principle or severity rating; its tag line carries '#non-toxic for cats', '#non-toxic for horses' and '#non-toxic for dogs'. RHS's dedicated page for the same shrub, filed as Potentilla fruticosa, has a 'Potentially harmful' row that reads: 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers'. The two sources differ: NC State tags the plant non-toxic for cats, horses and dogs, while RHS says the fruit is not to be eaten, repeats that under 'Pets:' without naming any animal, and adds a handling warning. Neither source lists symptoms or a toxic principle.
unknowns: NC State's dedicated Dasiphora fruticosa page is the anchor for every field. At audit, RHS's dedicated Potentilla fruticosa page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/13582/potentilla-fruticosa/details) and MoBot's Potentilla fruticosa page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286391; it refuses this machine, so none of its text is cited) were also read. They corroborate the sun list (RHS Position 'Full sun, Partial shade'; MoBot 'Sun: Full sun to part shade') and the size (MoBot 'Height: 2.00 to 4.00 feet', 'Spread: 3.00 to 5.00 feet'; RHS's Max Height and Max Spread read 1-1.5 metres and its description says 'slowly reaching 1.5m'), and RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained' agrees with soil_drainage moderate. MoBot's 'Water: Medium' row and its line 'Prefers evenly moist soils.' state no watering cadence, so water_regime stays null. MoBot's page is titled Potentilla fruticosa and its Common Name field reads 'shrubby cinquefoil', like RHS's lead. RHS adds a fruit and handling caution, recorded under toxicity_detail. RHS's Cultivation line 'Grow in any moisture-retentive soil in good light' is not read as moisture_retentive: it states no consistently wet requirement, and RHS's own structured Moisture field reads Moist but well–drained. Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA were not consulted.

humidity_need left null: NC State says only that this plant 'struggles in the high-humidity conditions of the southeastern United States' and that mildew can be an issue in the humid southern states. That is a regional climate warning, not a stated humidity level or enum value.

water_regime left null: NC State has no watering statement and no structured moisture field. 'Usually found in sunny, moist thickets and wet prairies' is a wild-habitat sentence, and 'drought-tolerant' is a tolerance trait; neither is a watering instruction. The structured Soil Drainage field (Good Drainage + Moist) governs soil_drainage only.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) together, so the range is open at both ends and no closed bound is stated. RHS's pH field for this shrub reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so RHS also accepts alkaline soil and no ceiling can be set.

toxicity: NC State has no Poison block; its only toxicity statement is the tags '#non-toxic for cats', '#non-toxic for horses' and '#non-toxic for dogs', with no symptoms or poison parts. RHS's Potentially harmful row says 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten.' and 'Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.', and its 'Pets:' line names no animal, so it supports neither value of toxic_to_pets; toxic_to_pets=false rests on NC State's cat- and dog-specific tags, and the RHS text is carried in toxicity_detail.

is_edible left null: NC State does not address eating this plant, and no admissible page read says any part is grown or used for food. RHS's page for this shrub has a Potentially harmful row reading 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten.', but RHS renders the identical row on its herbaceous Potentilla nepalensis page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/25565/potentilla-nepalensis/details), so it reads as a genus-wide caution about the fruit; it is carried in toxicity_detail rather than used to set is_edible.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's species prose says 'planting in full sun is preferred' and that it 'can be planted in part shade' without giving hours; the 6-hour and 2-6 hour figures are the site-wide light-legend ranges and were not used.
outdoor_sun_exposure: part_shade comes from NC State's structured 'Partial Shade' entry and its prose that the plant can be planted in part shade, with full sun preferred for best flowering.

soil_drainage: NC State's habitat sentence ('sunny, moist thickets and wet prairies') was not used; the value comes from the structured Good Drainage + Moist pair. The prose says it tolerates 'a wide range of well-drained soils'.
Fertilizer, temperature, humidity percentage, light footcandle and watering-interval fields have no support on the NC State page and are null.
chill_damage_f left null: NC State's Zones 3 to 7 and zones 2a-7b are hardiness ratings, not a damage-onset temperature.
